Each entry gets its key, its source file’s basename as group, and any class: key renamed to cls — all inside _load_registry, L287, which also rejects duplicate ids and reserved keywords.

Name resolution is the clever part. A registry entry may be a plain string or a dict containing an id, which is just an alias for another entry; _dereference, L156 follows that alias chain until it lands on a real spec, then constructs the typed dataclass. When the CLI asks for an eval that does not exist, the error message is genuinely helpful: difflib.get_close_matches suggests the nearest five ids. Class instantiation happens later via make_object, invoked from get_class, L153, which imports module:Class strings like evals.elsuite.basic.match:Match and injects the spec’s args.

The same machinery serves models. make_completion_fn, L120 recognizes three kinds of names: the literal dummy (a canned DummyCompletionFn, L48 — invaluable for testing without spending tokens), a chat model id like gpt-3.5-turbo detected by is_chat_model, L83, or anything else, looked up as a completion-fn or solver spec and instantiated. Context windows come from a hard-coded table in n_ctx_from_model_name, L37 — a snapshot whose comment honestly dates itself: “Model list last updated 2023-10-24.”

The Detail Map: One Run, End to End

The detail map follows one run: oaieval resolves the eval spec through the registry, the Eval base class fans samples over a thread pool, each sample calls a CompletionFn or a Solver, and match, sampling, and metric events stream into the recorder's JSONL log.

Eval, SolverEval, and the Sample Loop

evals/eval.py defines the contract every evaluation implements. The docstring on Eval, L46 is candid: a subclass overrides two methods — eval_sample, abstract at eval_sample, L77, and run, abstract at run, L86. The constructor takes the resolved completion functions, a registry path, a seed (default 20220722), and the eval’s dotted name, which must have at least a base_eval.split shape.

The fan-out is where the framework earns its keep. _index_samples, L30 shuffles sample indices with a fixed SHUFFLE_SEED of 123 — so runs are comparable even when the caller’s seed changes — and honors a global cap set by set_max_samples, L41 from the CLI’s --max_samples flag. Then eval_all_samples, L112 maps work items over a ThreadPool sized by EVALS_THREADS (default 10), or runs sequentially under EVALS_SEQUENTIAL. Per sample, it binds f"{base}.{split}.{idx}" as a sample id and enters as_default_recorder, L90, a context manager exposing the recorder and sample id through contextvars — which is why deep inside a completion function you can call the module-level record_sampling and it lands in the right place. Samples load via get_jsonl, L120, resolved against the registry’s data directory.

The newer sibling SolverEval, L168 inverts the model: instead of calling a completion function per prompt, it evaluates a Solver, L41 — an agent-like object that receives a TaskState, L24 with a task description, message history, and arbitrary state. SolverEval deep-copies the solver per sample so stateful solvers cannot contaminate each other, and via EVALS_GENTLE_INTERRUPT a Ctrl-C still reports metrics over the samples already finished.

Scoring primitives live in evals/api.py. record_and_check_match, L55 implements the workhorse pattern: prefix-match the sampled text against the expected option(s), require a separator after the prefix if one is defined, and record a match event with expected, picked, and sampled fields. Aggregation happens in evals/metrics.py: get_accuracy, L12 averages the correct flags of match events, while get_bootstrap_accuracy_std, L21 resamples half the events a thousand times to estimate the error bar next to every accuracy number.

CompletionFns, Solvers, and Prompt Formatting

The CompletionFn, L23 protocol is deliberately tiny: a callable taking a prompt (a string or a list of role/content messages) and returning a CompletionResult with get_completions(). The concrete OpenAI implementations wrap the openai client with a hand-rolled retry loop — OPENAI_TIMEOUT_EXCEPTIONS at L19 lists rate limits, connection errors, timeouts, and server errors, and both openai_completion_create_retrying, L27 and openai_chat_completion_create_retrying, L41 retry through it. After each call they record a sampling event including the raw usage, which the CLI later sums into per-run token counts.

Prompt formatting is its own small module. evals/prompt/base.py defines two type aliases — OpenAICreatePrompt, L15 for legacy completions and OpenAICreateChatPrompt, L19 for chat messages — plus two adapter dataclasses: CompletionPrompt, L86 renders a chat log down to User: / Assistant: prefixed text via chat_prompt_to_text_prompt, L22, and ChatCompletionPrompt, L103 lifts a plain string into a single system message. One eval body can thus serve both text-davinci-003-era and chat-era models without branching. Multiple-choice harnesses also get make_abc, L8 for shuffled A) B) C) option strings.

Solvers extend the protocol toward agents. Solver, L41 subclasses CompletionFn (so the registry treats both uniformly) and implements __call__ to deepcopy the task state, run the abstract _solve, then chain any configured PostProcessors — Strip, L5 and friends — over the output, recording each transformation. Composition is handled by NestedSolver, L137, which validates sub-solver specs and caches instances, plus recipes like CoTSolver, L9 and provider solvers such as OpenAISolver, L22. This is the natural seam for tool-using agents: a solver that calls tools shaped like the mcp-python-sdk contract plugs in without changing the eval that grades it.

Model-graded evals — where one model judges another — tie the stack together. ModelBasedClassify, L14 fetches a ModelGradedSpec, L12 from the registry (choice strings, input/output mappings, a prompt template), generates the completions under test, and asks the last completion function in the list to classify them; metaeval mode even grades the grader. Because these evals are pure YAML plus a shared class, the README notes this is currently the only contribution path — custom-code evals are not being accepted.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps setup short: pip install -e . from a clone (Python 3.9 minimum), or pip install evals if you only want to run existing evals, with OPENAI_API_KEY exported beforehand. One gotcha: the sample datasets under evals/registry/data use Git-LFS, so a fresh clone shows pointer files until you run git lfs fetch --all; git lfs pull.

Your first run then needs two positional arguments — a completion function name and an eval name — as declared by get_parser, L25:

oaieval gpt-3.5-turbo test-match

That resolves test-match through the registry, instantiates Match, and writes a JSONL log to the default path /tmp/evallogs/{run_id}_{model}_{eval}.jsonl unless --record_path overrides it. Flags worth knowing: --max_samples 20 for a cheap smoke test, --dry_run to swap in the console-only DummyRecorder, --registry_path for your own YAML, and --extra_eval_params for per-eval settings like num_few_shot. The recorder choice is made in build_recorder, L242: local JSONL by default, an HttpRecorder posting batched events under --http-run, or the Snowflake-backed Recorder for OpenAI-internal dashboards. When the run ends, the CLI prints the final report and add_token_usage_to_result, L269 folds summed token counts into it. For suites, oaievalset expands an eval-set YAML into oaieval subprocess commands with checkpointed resume, driven from run, L81.

Honest Limits

Three facts from the README frame your expectations. First, the README’s opening banner points you to configure and run evals “directly in the OpenAI Dashboard” — the project’s center of gravity has moved to a hosted product, and the team is currently not accepting evals with custom code; only model-graded YAML contributions are reviewed. Second, several pillars are frozen in time: the registry’s context-window table is annotated as last updated 2023-10-24, and the completion functions target the openai client of that era — bring your own CompletionFn (the protocol makes that a small class) for newer endpoints or local servers. Third, the Snowflake recorder and its environment variables exist for OpenAI’s internal use; external users realistically use the local JSONL path — the format is just newline-delimited Event dicts with a spec header and a final_report trailer.

None of that diminishes the framework’s value as a blueprint. The registry’s name-to-class indirection, the sample-id-scoped recorder context, and the CompletionFn seam are patterns you can lift into any evaluation stack — including the community harness compared in lm-eval-harness. And the lineage runs deep: many registry datasets still reference completions from the gpt-2 era, when “evaluation” meant perplexity and exact match.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of openai/evals — the registry engine, the Eval base classes, completion functions, model-graded grading, and the oaieval runner.

entry.title: pgvector Source Tour: How Vector Search Lives Inside Postgres

link.title: pgvector Source Tour: How Vector Search Lives Inside Postgres

entry.content:
Every retrieval-augmented application eventually faces the same storage question: where do the embeddings live? Many teams end up syncing a vector file with a relational database, and paying for two systems that drift apart. pgvector takes the opposite approach: it is a compact C extension, currently at version 0.8.7, that teaches PostgreSQL itself to store vectors and search them by similarity. Because it runs inside the database, your embeddings inherit everything Postgres already does well — ACID transactions, write-ahead logging, point-in-time recovery, JOINs, and any client language with a Postgres driver.

The feature list is longer than the codebase suggests. pgvector supports exact and approximate nearest neighbor search, four storage types (single-precision vector, half-precision halfvec, bit, and sparsevec), and six distance metrics: L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming, and Jaccard. Two index types cover the approximate side — HNSW, a multi-layer proximity graph that is the recommended default, and IVFFlat, the classic inverted-file approach with k-means clustering. There is no Python here at all; it is plain C compiled against the PostgreSQL server headers, which is exactly why a source tour is so readable.

This post walks that source tree from master, with every symbol and line number verified against the working tree. Two diagrams were generated for it: an overview of how the pieces connect, and a detail map of the two index access methods. The post also shows the LLM tooling side of the ecosystem elsewhere on this site, but first, let’s see what 28 files under src/ actually do.

pgvector at a glance: the SQL catalog wires a varlena type and two index access methods to C callbacks; both index types funnel into the same distance kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • vector_in, L178 parses the textual form '[1,2,3]' with strtof, rejects NaN and Infinity, and enforces the declared dimension through CheckExpectedDim at L274 — that is how vector(3) refuses a 4-element literal. The struct it fills in lives in vector.h, L18: a varlena header, an int16 dimension, and a flexible float array, capped at 16,000 dimensions (VECTOR_MAX_DIM, L11).
  • l2_distance, L581 and its siblings — inner_product, L624, cosine_distance, L673, l1_distance, L742 — are plain loops the compiler auto-vectorizes. They back the operators <->, <#>, <=>, and <+> declared in vector.sql, L254.
  • hnswhandler, L468 fills PostgreSQL’s IndexAmRoutine struct: ambuild points at hnswbuild, aminsert at hnswinsert, amgettuple at hnswgettuple. This is the standard index access method interface, so CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw needs no special syntax.
  • hnswbuild, L1166 runs a two-phase build. The graph first lives entirely in memory; when it no longer fits in maintenance_work_mem, FlushPages, L297 materializes what exists and the build switches to inserting tuples one by one, WAL-free, exactly like normal inserts.
  • hnswinsert, L836 is the per-row hook. HnswInsertTuple, L817 picks neighbors level by level, from the top of the hierarchy down, then links the new element into each layer.
  • HnswSearchLayer, L1017 is the shared greedy beam search used by both inserts and queries. At query time hnswgettuple, L197 drives it with a candidate list sized by hnsw.ef_search, 40 by default (HNSW_DEFAULT_EF_SEARCH, L71).
  • ivfflatbuild, L1058 samples the table, clusters it, and delegates the math to IvfflatKmeans, L554, which uses the Elkan triangle-inequality trick (ElkanKmeans, L247) to skip most distance recomputations between iterations.
  • ivfflatgettuple, L364 scans only the lists whose centers are closest to the query — ivfflat.probes of them, 1 by default (IVFFLAT_DEFAULT_PROBES, L56).

Two Index Access Methods Under One Extension

The elegant part of pgvector’s design is how little custom machinery it needs beyond the PostgreSQL extension points. In sql/vector.sql, the type is declared at L6, then the two access methods with just two lines each: CREATE ACCESS METHOD ivfflat TYPE INDEX HANDLER ivfflathandler at L355 and CREATE ACCESS METHOD hnsw TYPE INDEX HANDLER hnswhandler at L364. Everything else — build, insert, scan, vacuum, cost estimation — is the AM author filling in a function-pointer table. hnswhandler even declares .amcanbuildparallel = true, which is why large HNSW builds can use parallel workers.

Operator classes do the semantic gluing. vector_l2_ops binds <-> to l2_distance, vector_cosine_ops binds <=> to cosine_distance, and so on for each storage type, so one C function such as l2_distance serves both plain queries and index scans. Because Postgres only supports ascending index scans on operators, <#> returns the negative inner product — a small but important subtlety when you multiply by -1 to recover the true similarity.

Inside the Detail Diagram

The detail map zooms into the two AMs and the type layer. It is worth reading top to bottom if you plan to modify the index code:

The detail graph: on-disk format structs in hnsw.h and ivfflat.h, the shared HnswSearchLayer core, and the k-means stage that only IVFFlat pays for.

  • CreateMetaPage, L82 stamps the metapage with a magic number, the fixed dimensions, m, ef_construction, and the entry point. The persistence format is defined by HnswMetaPageData at L347 and the element and neighbor tuple layouts at L371 and L385.
  • HnswGetMetaPageInfo, L312 reads that metadata back on every scan and insert, while HnswUpdateMetaPageInfo, L363 advances the entry point as the graph grows taller.
  • HnswInsertTupleOnDisk, L760 wraps each page modification in GenericXLog, which is the reason HNSW indexes replicate and support point-in-time recovery like any other index.
  • hnswbulkdelete, L793 and hnswvacuumcleanup, L818 keep dead heap tuples from polluting search results during VACUUM.
  • ivfflatoptions, L172 validates the lists reloption against the 32,768 ceiling (IVFFLAT_MAX_LISTS, L55); the k-means stage is why IVFFlat needs data before you can build the index, while HNSW’s hnswbuildempty, L1184 happily creates an index on an empty table.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quick start is honest about the compile step, and it is the right place to start. On Linux or Mac, with Postgres 13 or newer:

git clone --branch v0.8.7 https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector.git
cd pgvector
make
make install # may need sudo

Windows builds through an x64 Native Tools Command Prompt with nmake /F Makefile.win, and there are Docker, Homebrew, APT, Yum, and PGXN packages if you would rather not compile. Once the extension is on the server, everything else is plain SQL:

CREATE EXTENSION vector;

CREATE TABLE items (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, embedding vector(3));
INSERT INTO items (embedding) VALUES ('[1,2,3]'), ('[4,5,6]');

CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops);

SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;

Four lines worth unpacking. CREATE EXTENSION vector runs vector.sql and registers the type, operators, and both access methods in one transaction. vector(3) fixes the dimension through the typmod path (vector_typmod_in at L343), so a mismatched insert fails immediately instead of silently. The CREATE INDEX line builds an HNSW graph over the column; add one index per metric you query (vector_ip_ops, vector_cosine_ops, vector_l1_ops). And the final SELECT combines ORDER BY with a distance operator and LIMIT — that trio is what lets the planner choose an index scan instead of a sequential scan over every row.

Tuning is two knobs. Before the query: SET hnsw.ef_search = 100 enlarges the candidate list for better recall at the cost of speed. Before the build: m (16 by default, HNSW_DEFAULT_M, L65) and ef_construction (64 by default) trade build time and memory against graph quality. The README’s advice — index after bulk-loading, raise maintenance_work_mem so the in-memory build phase does not spill — falls straight out of the build code we read above.

Storage Types, Distances, and Quantization

The vector type stores 4 bytes per dimension plus an 8-byte header, with a hard limit of 16,000 dimensions but an index limit of 2,000 (HNSW_MAX_DIM, L43). The companion types attack that ceiling from both ends. halfvec halves storage with 2-byte elements and indexes up to 4,000 dimensions; its distance math lives in the SIMD helpers of halfutils.c, L47. sparsevec stores {index:value}/dim pairs for text-heavy workloads where only a few components are nonzero. And binary quantization indexes up to 64,000 dimensions by hashing each vector to bits, then re-ranking with the original floats — a two-stage pattern you can express entirely in SQL with expression indexes.

Metric choice matters more than most people expect. If your embedding model produces unit-normalized vectors (common for OpenAI-style embeddings), inner product search and cosine search return the same ordering, and inner product is cheaper. Cosine distance is the safe default otherwise. This matters when comparing pgvector with dedicated in-process libraries like USearch or FAISS: the graph algorithms are cousins (USearch also uses HNSW), but pgvector’s payoff is transactional co-location with your rows, not raw in-memory throughput.

The practical integration point is upstream: whatever generates the embeddings — a sentence-transformer served via Transformers, or a locally trained tokenizer — writes floats into INSERT statements, and retrieval happens with one operator in a WHERE clause alongside your other filters.

Honest Limits

  • Approximate means approximate. An HNSW index trades recall for speed, and results can differ between queries after the index exists. Filters are applied after the index scan, so a highly selective WHERE clause can return fewer rows than requested; 0.8.0’s iterative index scans mitigate this by scanning more of the index when needed, bounded by hnsw.max_scan_tuples (20,000 by default).
  • The 2,000-dimension index ceiling is real. Beyond it you must use half-precision indexing (4,000), binary quantization (64,000), subvector indexing, or dimensionality reduction. The type itself stores 16,000 dimensions, but those rows will not be indexed as-is.
  • Vacuum on HNSW is slow. The README itself recommends REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY before VACUUM on large HNSW indexes — the graph structure makes bulk deletion expensive.
  • No built-in sharding or ANN benchmarks are provided. The project scales vertically, with replicas, or via external sharding examples; there are no published QPS or recall figures in the repository, and any numbers you see elsewhere are someone else’s benchmark, not the project’s.
  • The README’s own recommendation: monitor recall by comparing approximate results against exact search with SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off, and use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before tuning anything.

What makes pgvector compelling is not that it beats a GPU index library on raw speed — it does not try to. It is that the entire approximate search engine, from hnswhandler down to the WAL-logged page tuples, fits in a directory you can read in an afternoon, and it deploys wherever Postgres already runs. For teams whose embeddings must live beside their transactions, that combination is hard to beat.

entry.title: txtai Source Tour: Inside the Embeddings Database Engine

link.title: txtai Source Tour: Inside the Embeddings Database Engine

entry.content:
Most vector-search libraries hand you an index and stop there. txtai, from NeuML, takes the wider view: it is an embeddings database — a Python platform where you index text, documents, audio, images and video, keep the original content in SQL, link records into a graph network, and then query everything semantically, lexically, or through LLM-driven agents. The README’s pitch is refreshingly blunt: up and running in minutes with pip, run local so your data never leaves the machine, scale up only when you need to.

I spent an afternoon walking the source tree on the master branch. txtai targets Python 3.11+ and is built on Hugging Face Transformers, Sentence Transformers and FastAPI, all under an Apache 2.0 license. What struck me most is how small the core object graph is: one Embeddings facade owns every subsystem, and each subsystem gets its own package with a tiny factory that reads your YAML config. The two diagrams below were generated directly from the code paths I traced, and every node in them links back to the exact file and line in the repository — so you can treat this post as a map and jump straight into the code whenever something looks interesting.

This is a read-order tour: the engine first, then the storage and scoring plumbing underneath it, then the runtime layer that turns a local index into an API service, a task graph, or an agent’s memory.

txtai at a glance: the Embeddings facade on the left, its vectorization and storage subsystems in the middle, and the serving, orchestration and agent runtimes on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right

  • Embeddings is the center of gravity. The class holds every handle the engine needs — ann, database, graph, scoring, model — and exposes the verbs you actually call: index() at L102, upsert() at L154, search() at L355 and similarity() at L405.
  • Vectors is the vectorization base class: index() at L119 batches documents, transform() at L205 converts one document into a similarity vector. The VectorsFactory picks a concrete backend, with STVectors wrapping sentence-transformers models as the everyday choice.
  • ANN is the vector index wrapper: append() at L51 ingests vectors, search() at L71 runs batched nearest-neighbor queries. The ANNFactory selects the backend — the zero-dependency NumPy scan, Faiss, or HNSW via hnswlib.
  • Database is the content store: insert() at L43 writes rows, search() at L116 executes SQL with similarity ordering. The SQLite backend is the default, and DatabaseFactory also supports server RDBMS options.
  • Scoring powers lexical and sparse retrieval: TFIDF at ScoringFactory, BM25 extending TFIDF, and the Sparse backend for learned sparse embeddings.
  • Graph builds a relationship network over indexed rows via GraphFactory, enabling path queries, topic modeling and graph-enhanced ranking.
  • Workflow orchestrates callable tasks as a DAG; __call__() at L51 streams elements through it, backed by the Execute scheduler.
  • Agent is the LLM loop: __call__() at L67 runs tool-augmented sessions whose tools are your own embeddings instances and task graphs, assembled by ProcessFactory.
  • API extends Application to serve a configured index over HTTP; create() at L32 assembles the FastAPI app that uvicorn runs. There is also a Console REPL for poking at an index interactively.

The engine’s two paths

Almost everything in txtai happens along two paths. The indexing path starts at Embeddings.index(): documents stream in through a Stream helper, each one goes to the vector model, the resulting vectors are appended to the ANN index, the raw content is inserted into the database, term weights land in the scoring index, and — if you enabled graph support — relationships are linked as it goes. The query path starts at Embeddings.search(): the query is vectorized, the ANN returns candidate neighbors, the database applies SQL where-clauses and joins content back, and hybrid mode fuses the dense ranking with the sparse one.

That hybrid search is worth pausing on. The Hybrid class blends dense vector results with sparse scoring results, which is how txtai gets both “matches the meaning” and “matches the exact keyword” behavior from one call. Dense retrieval alone is famously bad at rare terms — product codes, error strings, names — and a BM25 term index alone misses paraphrases. txtai runs both and merges the rankings, and the whole mechanism lives in one small file you can read in minutes.

The third interesting path is explanation. Embeddings.explain() at L446 annotates results with the terms that drove the match, which sounds cosmetic until you have to debug why a query keeps surfacing the wrong documents — then it is the difference between guessing and knowing.

The detail view: configuration factories on the left build the concrete backends, the index and search paths wire them together, and the workflow, agent and API runtimes sit on top.

Backends everywhere, config decides

The detail diagram makes txtai’s design philosophy obvious: every subsystem is an interface plus a factory plus N interchangeable backends. Dense vectors come from sentence-transformers (STVectors) or an ONNX encoder graph for optimized inference — the same model-serialization trick we covered in our ONNX runtime tour, and a reminder of how far a quantized encoder graph goes. ANN indexes come from NumPy, faiss, or HNSW, and there is even a pgvector option for teams that want Postgres to own the vectors — our pgvector walkthrough covers that side of the world. Content lives in SQLite by default or in an external RDBMS.

Because every backend is chosen by a factory reading your YAML config, swapping faiss for hnswlib or SQLite for Postgres is a configuration edit, not a code change. The factories are all tiny — ANNFactory at L22, ScoringFactory at L15, DatabaseFactory at L15, GraphFactory at L12 — and they follow the same registry shape, so once you have read one you have effectively read them all.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything below is straight from the README, and it genuinely is two lines before you have a working semantic index.

First, install the package:

pip install txtai

Then build and query an index in Python:

# Get started in a couple lines
import txtai

embeddings = txtai.Embeddings()
embeddings.index(["Correct", "Not what we hoped"])
embeddings.search("positive", 1)
# [(0, 0.29862046241760254)]

No model name, no vector dimension, no preprocessing script: the defaults pick a sentence-transformers encoder, download it on first use, and vectorize your documents. The returned tuple is the document id and its similarity score — 0 is the id of "Correct", the only positive sentence in the corpus.

The second way to run txtai is as a service. Point a YAML file at the model and start uvicorn:

# app.yml
embeddings:
    path: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2

CONFIG=app.yml uvicorn "txtai.api:app"
curl -X GET "http://localhost:8000/search?query=positive"

That is the whole deployment story for a single-node instance: the YAML config instantiates the same Embeddings object you built in Python, and the FastAPI application exposes search over HTTP. From there the config can declare workflows, agents and more, all served by the same process — the README’s stated model is “simple microservices or multi-model workflows” joined by task graphs.

Workflows and agents: the engine as a component

The runtime layer is where txtai stops being a library and starts being a platform. A Workflow is a set of tasks with declared connections; WorkflowFactory at L9 — loaded from config — and the Execute engine at L13 stream elements through the graph, scheduling independent tasks in parallel. The tasks themselves are ordinary callables: a transcription model, a summarizer, an embeddings index — each one consumes the output of the previous stage. In other words, the “workflow tasks” in the YAML are component runners over txtai’s own processing tasks, and the API service exposes them as HTTP endpoints.

An Agent then closes the loop: it wraps an LLM, binds tools — your embeddings instances, your workflows, even other agents — and runs the tool-augmented reasoning loop in __call__() at L67. A retrieval-augmented generation system stops being a script you wrote and becomes a named process with a config entry, which is exactly what you want once a second application needs the same behavior. The README also documents web and MCP APIs, with bindings for JavaScript, Java, Rust and Go, so the same index can back a web app, a chat client and an MCP-connected assistant.

This layered shape — one engine, many task graphs over it, agents on top — is the same trajectory we saw in our LlamaIndex tour, but txtai arrives at it from the database direction rather than the framework direction, and the difference shows in how little ceremony surrounds the engine itself. The Transformers substrate underneath is the same one we walked through in our Transformers architecture post.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you build on it, all verifiable in the source or README:

  • Writes need synchronization. The Embeddings docstring at L31 states it plainly: indexes are thread-safe for read operations, but writes must be synchronized by your application. Reads can scale across threads; a concurrent write strategy is your problem to coordinate.
  • Python 3.11+ only. The README is explicit about the floor, so older environments need to upgrade first.
  • The batteries-included core pulls real dependencies. A minimal install gets you far, but the README also advertises a low footprint with optional extras — the trade is that faiss, hnswlib, audio, video and LLM integrations are additional installs you opt into per feature.
  • First use downloads models. The default path needs a sentence-transformers encoder, so the very first index build involves a model download; offline environments must pre-seed the model cache.
  • Quality is a function of your chosen encoder. txtai is model-agnostic, which means result quality tracks whatever embedding model you configure — the engine will faithfully organize whatever representations that model produces.
  • No benchmark theater. The README makes capability claims, not speed claims; for the numbers that matter you will want to run your own queries against your own corpus, which the example notebooks make straightforward.

None of these are disqualifying — they are the honest edges of a design that puts one very solid engine in the middle and lets configuration decide everything else. If your problem is “index my content, query it semantically, serve it over an API, and let an LLM reason over it,” the source shows a clean path from two lines of Python to exactly that.

entry.title: USearch Architecture: A Source Tour of Unum’s Single-Header Vector Search Engine

link.title: USearch Architecture: A Source Tour of Unum’s Single-Header Vector Search Engine

entry.content:
Most vector databases you encounter are services: a server process, a network protocol, a deployment story. USearch from Unum-cloud takes the opposite path. It is a single-file C++11 header — include/usearch/index.hpp — that implements a multi-layer proximity graph for approximate nearest neighbor search, and it ships as a library you link or import, not a cluster you operate. Despite the small footprint, it is embedded in production systems you already know: ClickHouse and DuckDB both use it as their native vector index, and the project reports being trusted by teams at Google as well.

The repository covers an unusually wide surface for its size: C++, C99, Python, Rust, Java, JavaScript, Go, Swift, C#, Objective-C, and even Wolfram bindings all build from the same three headers. That makes it a great codebase to read if you want to understand how a real ANN engine is layered: a templated graph core, a type-punning layer that erases vector dtypes at runtime, and a stack of native bindings that each do their own FFI rather than relying on generated wrappers. In this tour we walk through that architecture with two diagrams, then get hands-on with the Python interface.

The overview below maps the whole system. On the left are the three public headers and how they include each other; in the middle, the runtime objects those headers define; on the right, the language bindings and the on-disk format that makes indexes portable between languages.

USearch overview: headers on the left define the runtime objects in the center; bindings consume the dense facade, and the serialization layer persists 64-byte-headed binary files.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • index.hpp, L1 is the self-contained C++11 core. It needs no sibling includes and starts by detecting compiler, OS, and ISA macros, then defines version macros like USEARCH_VERSION_MAJOR, L10.
  • index_gt, L2291 is the proximity graph itself: a template over key and slot types that owns the node tape, striped locks, and per-thread contexts. Its add, L3219 inserts through greedy descent, and its search, L3468 walks the layers down before refining candidates.
  • index_plugins.hpp, L12 includes the core and extends it with the distance machinery: metric_kind_t, L115 enumerates cos, ip, l2sq, hamming, tanimoto, jaccard, haversine and more, while scalar_kind_t, L140 covers every storage dtype from f64 down to single-bit b1x8 and float8 e5m2/e4m3.
  • metric_punned_t, L2894 is the runtime metric dispatcher. Its builtin, L2954 factory selects an ISA-specialized kernel, and its stateless, L2984 factory wraps a raw function pointer — the hook that makes user-defined metrics possible.
  • index_dense.hpp, L406 defines index_dense_gt, the type-erased facade most users actually touch: it stores a casts_punned_t caster so an f16 index can accept f32 queries, and exposes typed add/search overloads like add(f32...), L873 and search(f32...), L885.
  • The Python binding python/lib.cpp, L1126 is a hand-written pybind11 module declared GIL-free. It exposes the Index class, L1251 with batch entry points add_many, L1269 and search_many, L1280.
  • The Rust binding rust/lib.rs, L668 takes a different route: a cxx bridge to a NativeIndex object, with a safe wrapper exposing search at L1449 and add at L1507.
  • On the storage side, index_dense_head_t, L42 is the 64-byte header that begins every serialized index, so a file written from Python can be memory-mapped from C++ or Rust.

Inside the Dense Layer

The detail diagram drills one level deeper, and it is where USearch’s design philosophy — “punning” — becomes visible. The graph core index_gt is a template: at compile time it works with whatever value and metric types you instantiate it with. But Python cannot instantiate C++ templates at runtime. So index_dense_gt erases all of that behind runtime state: a metric dispatcher, a caster table, and a pointer to the typed instantiation.

Detail view: the graph core (top), metrics and dtypes (left), the dense punning layer with its factory, insert, query, and serialization paths (center), and the Python and Rust binding internals (bottom).

Follow the search flow through the center of the diagram. A call into the dense facade lands on the per-dtype overload, which delegates to the private search_, L2242. That function casts your query buffer into the index’s native dtype using the caster, builds an index_search_config_t, L1728 carrying the per-query expansion and exact flag, and finally calls into the graph with a small closure as a predicate. That closure is the key trick: even the base graph’s search accepts an arbitrary predicate, so filtered search composes naturally instead of being bolted on. The public filtered_search, L897 overloads simply pass a user predicate through where the default path passes one that skips deleted keys.

Insertion works symmetrically. The dense add_, L2178 first tries to pop a free slot from the recycled-slots structure — deletions in USearch mark keys as free rather than rebuilding the graph — then allocates vector storage, registers the key-to-slot mapping, and calls either the graph’s add or its update path depending on whether a slot was recycled. The hierarchy itself is standard HNSW: nodes live on multiple levels, and level_of, L2838 reads how high a given slot reaches. When exactness matters more than speed, exact=true routes around the graph entirely into search_exact_, L4796, a brute-force scan.

Serialization is the third pillar. save, L1594 and load, L1601 accept paths, streams, or buffers, and view, L1353 memory-maps an existing file without loading it into RAM — the property the README credits with order-of-magnitude serving cost reductions on cloud block storage. The factory method make, L663 mirrors this: it constructs either from a metric configuration or directly from a file path with a view flag.

From Install to Your First Model

The Python package is on PyPI under the name usearch, and the whole first-run experience fits in a dozen lines:

# pip install usearch
import numpy as np
from usearch.index import Index

index = Index(ndim=384, metric="cos", dtype="bf16")
vectors = np.random.rand(10_000, 384).astype(np.float32)
index.add(keys=np.arange(10_000), vectors=vectors)

query = np.random.rand(384).astype(np.float32)
matches = index.search(query, 10)
print(matches[0].key, matches[0].distance)

Three defaults are worth knowing. The metric defaults to cosine; the dtype is chosen per hardware — the wrapper documents that nothing is stored as f32 unless you ask, because bf16 or f16 is nearly always the better trade-off on modern CPUs. And connectivity (the HNSW paper’s “M”) defaults to a compiled-in constant exposed by the module, as do the two expansion factors: expansion_add (the paper’s efConstruction) and expansion_search (ef), both changeable after construction through properties on the Index.

A realistic embedding workflow looks like this: encode your corpus with a sentence-embedding model — the same pattern used by sentence-transformers-style encoders or CLIP for multimodal data — add the vectors under your own integer keys, and keep the mapping from keys to documents in your application. Serialization then becomes one call, and the wrapper class wraps the C++ paths for save, L1101, load, and read-only view:

index.save("corpus.usearch")

# Later, on a serving box, without paying the RAM bill:
disk_index = Index(ndim=384, metric="cos", path="corpus.usearch", view=True)

For retrieval-augmented generation systems, this is the entire ANN layer: a few megabytes of compiled code, no server, and an index format you can ship alongside your model weights. Projects like LlamaIndex can sit on top of it, and if you export encoders through ONNX you can keep the whole serving stack free of framework dependencies.

Metrics, Quantization, and User-Defined Distances

USearch’s metric story is broader than the usual cosine/L2 pair. Spatial metrics (cos, ip, l2sq), binary coefficients (hamming, tanimoto, sorensen, jaccard), and even geographic haversine are built in, and the README leans into the unusual ones — molecular search over RDKit fingerprints and geo point-clouds are showcased applications.

Quantization follows a “downcast, don’t train” philosophy. Instead of learned product quantization, the same add and search calls transparently convert between f64, f32, bf16, f16, the float8 formats e5m2/e4m3, the float6 pair e3m2/e2m3, i8, u8, and single-bit b1x8, using SIMD paths when the hardware has them. You can check what your CPU gets with Index(ndim=768, metric="cos", dtype="f16").hardware_acceleration, which reports the ISA name the dispatcher selected. For quarter-precision, the README notes the constraints: i8 is only valid for cosine-like metrics and normalizes vectors to unit length before scaling, while b1x8 is only valid for binary metrics.

When none of the built-ins fit, the stateless, L2984 constructor path is exposed all the way up to Python as CompiledMetric: compile a Numba cfunc with the right signature, hand USearch its address, and the graph traverses with your distance. Because the search only requires comparable distances — not identical vector lengths — this opens genuinely odd use cases, like gzip-compression-ratio as a similarity function for fuzzy text matching.

Filtering, Clustering, and Joins

Filtered search deserves emphasis because most engines get it wrong. The naive approach retrieves top-k then filters, which falls apart when the filter is selective. USearch instead evaluates your predicate during graph traversal — every candidate is checked before it can enter the result set — and the README’s position is that predicates should compose with external containers like Bloom filters. Note the language support split though: the functionality table in the README shows filter predicates supported in C++, C, Rust, and Swift, but not yet in Python; in Python you filter after retrieval.

The same graph doubles as a clustering engine. index.cluster(min_count=..., max_count=...) produces a Clustering object with centroid popularity, per-cluster membership, and iterative sub-clustering, which the README positions against SciPy-style hierarchical clustering at much larger scale. Finally, Index.join computes stable-marriage-style one-to-one mappings between two indexes — fuzzy joins with sub-quadratic complexity — a database-flavored feature almost no other ANN library offers.

Honest Limits

Reading the source also clarifies what USearch is not, and every point below comes straight from the project’s own README and functionality table:

  • It is approximate by default. HNSW trades exactness for speed; the exact=True brute-force path exists, and the README reports it comparing well against FAISS’s IndexFlatL2 in a Colab setting, but for small datasets a plain numpy scan may serve you fine.
  • Performance claims are the project’s own. The headline “10x faster HNSW than FAISS” comes from Unum’s Intel-published benchmark on Sapphire Rapids with equivalent recall — not from an independent audit. Reproduce it on your data before trusting it.
  • Python lags C++ in features. No filter predicates, no joins in the other languages, no variable-length vectors outside C++, and 4B+-capacity uint40_t slots are C++-only per the functionality table.
  • Quantization is lossy and one-way. Once vectors are stored downcast, the “get”-style accessors cannot recover the original data — the README explicitly tells you to keep originals elsewhere if you need them.
  • No server, no replication, no consistency story. USearch is a library. Concurrency is handled inside the index (it is thread-safe for concurrent add and search), but durability, sharding, and multi-node serving are entirely your problem — that is what Indexes, the multi-index lookup wrapper, partially addresses by viewing several shard files as one.
  • Key management is on you. Keys are integers; mapping them to real-world entities, handling renames and deletions, and compacting after removals are explicit API calls, not background processes.

That trade is the whole appeal, though. If your problem fits in one process and one machine’s disk, USearch gives you a serious ANN engine in a dependency-free header, with an index format you can read back from ten languages. The full tour above — graph core, punning layer, bindings, and file format — fits in roughly 3,000 lines of C++, which is exactly why it is worth reading in an afternoon.
entry.summary: How the 3,000-line C++ core of USearch powers approximate nearest neighbor search across Python, Rust, and eight other languages - a guided source tour.
